statement: To find the second binomial straight line.
heath_proof: Let two numbers AC, CB be set out such that the sum of them AB has to BC the ratio which a square number has to a square number, but has not to AC the ratio which a square number has to a square number; let a rational straight line D be set out, and let EF be commensurable in length with D; therefore EF is rational. Let it be contrived then that, as the number CA is to AB, so also is the square on EF to the square on FG; [X. 6] therefore the square on EF is commensurable with the square on FG. [X. 6] Therefore FG is also rational. Now, since the number CA has not to AB the ratio which a square number has to a square number, neither has the square on EF to the square on FG the ratio which a square number has to a square number. Therefore EF is incommensurable in length with FG; [X. 9] therefore EF, FG are rational straight lines commensurable in square only; therefore EG is binomial. [X. 36] It is next to be proved that it is also a second binomial straight line. For since, inversely, as the number BA is to AC, so is the square on GF to the square on FE, while BA is greater than AC, therefore the square on GF is greater than the square on FE. Let the squares on EF, H be equal to the square on GF; therefore, convertendo, as AB is to BC, so is the square on FG to the square on H. [V. 19] But AB has to BC the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore the square on FG also has to the square on H the ratio which a square number has to a square number. Therefore FG is commensurable in length with H; [X. 9] so that the square on FG is greater than the square on FE by the square on a straight line commensurable with FG. And FG, FE are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, and EF, the lesser term, is commensurable in length with the rational straight line D set out. Therefore EG is a second binomial straight line.
ai_proof_text:
10.49
**Statement:** To find the second binomial straight line.

**Step 1.** Let D be the rational straight line set out (D10.1.3). Take two numbers AC, CB whose sum AB has to CB the ratio which a square number has to a square number, but has not to CA such a ratio: namely, let AB be the number 9, BC the number 4, and CA the number 5, so that AB is the sum of AC and CB. Since 9 is 3 multiplied by 3 and 4 is 2 multiplied by 2, AB and BC are square numbers (D7.18); therefore AB has to BC the ratio which a square number has to a square number. But AB has not to CA the ratio which a square number has to a square number: for if it had, then, AB being square, CA would also be square (8.24); but 5 is not a square number, since 2 by 2 makes 4 and 3 by 3 makes 9, and no number multiplied by itself makes 5.

**Step 2.** Let EF be a straight line commensurable in length with D. Then EF is rational (D10.1.3).

**Step 3.** Produce EF to G (P2) so that, as the number CA is to the number AB, so is the square on EF to the square on FG; this is possible by the Porism to 10.6 (a straight line X is found such that EF is to X as CA is to AB, and FG is taken as a mean proportional between EF and X, so that EF is to X as the square on EF is to the square on FG). Thus EG is one straight line divided at F.

**Step 4.** Since the square on EF has to the square on FG the ratio which the number CA has to the number AB, the square on EF is commensurable with the square on FG (10.6); that is, EF and FG are commensurable in square (D10.1.2).

**Step 5.** Since EF is commensurable in length with D, the square on EF has to the square on D the ratio which a square number has to a square number (10.9), and therefore the square on EF is commensurable with the square on D (10.6). But the square on FG is commensurable with the square on EF (Step 4). Therefore the square on FG is commensurable with the square on D (10.12), so that FG is commensurable in square with D and is therefore rational (D10.1.3).

**Step 6.** Since CA has not to AB the ratio which a square number has to a square number (Step 1), and the square on EF has to the square on FG the same ratio as CA has to AB (Step 3), neither has the square on EF to the square on FG the ratio which a square number has to a square number. Therefore EF is incommensurable in length with FG (10.9).

**Step 7.** Accordingly EF, FG are rational straight lines commensurable in square only (Steps 2, 4, 5, 6). Therefore EG, which is made up of them, is a binomial straight line, and EF, FG are its terms (10.36).

**Step 8.** Since, as CA is to AB, so is the square on EF to the square on FG, inversely, as AB is to CA, so is the square on FG to the square on EF (5.7 Porism). Now AB, being 9, is greater than CA, being 5. Take the same equimultiples of all four magnitudes, say the doubles: since AB is greater than CA, the double of AB exceeds the double of CA; hence, by the definition of magnitudes in the same ratio, the double of the square on FG exceeds the double of the square on EF (D5.5). Therefore the square on FG is greater than the square on EF, and consequently FG is greater than EF; so FG is the greater and EF the lesser of the two terms.

**Step 9.** On FG describe a semicircle FKG, and, since EF is less than FG, fit into it the straight line FK equal to EF (4.1); join KG (P1). The angle FKG, being in a semicircle, is right (3.31); therefore the square on FG is equal to the squares on FK, KG (1.47), that is, to the squares on EF, KG. Let H denote KG. Thus the square on FG is greater than the square on EF by the square on H.

**Step 10.** Since, as AB is to CA, so is the square on FG to the square on EF (Step 8), and AB exceeds CA by CB, while the square on FG exceeds the square on EF by the square on H (Step 9), convertendo, as AB is to BC, so is the square on FG to the square on H (5.19 Porism).

**Step 11.** But AB has to BC the ratio which a square number has to a square number (Step 1). Therefore the square on FG has to the square on H the ratio which a square number has to a square number, and hence FG is commensurable in length with H (10.9).

**Step 12.** Therefore EG is a binomial straight line divided into its terms EF, FG (Step 7); the square on the greater term FG is greater than the square on the lesser term EF by the square on H, a straight line commensurable in length with FG (Steps 9, 11); and the lesser term EF is commensurable in length with the rational straight line D set out (Step 2). Therefore EG is a second binomial straight line (D10.2.2). Thus the second binomial straight line EG has been found. Q.E.F.

**Path note.** The numbers were fixed explicitly (9, 4, 5) rather than by appeal to the unnumbered lemma after 10.28, and H was constructed by the semicircle method (the unnumbered lemma before 10.14) rather than cited, since lemmas carry no proposition numbers.
